description: The token sets SPEC.md names and expects an implementation to spell identically, published as data so a spelling can be generated or checked rather than transcribed. A derived view: the specification governs, this file restates no requirement's substance, and a disagreement is a bug here.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 10.4 "Emitted Runtime Events (Upstream to Orchestrator)"
events.note: The neutral event vocabulary every adapter MUST emit (Section 10.7). Not a closed set: Section 10.4 states that an adapter MAY emit additional events and that a consumer MUST tolerate an unrecognized name, so a generated type MUST admit an unknown token rather than closing the enum. The names are fixed for the conditions they do name.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 10.4 "Emitted Runtime Events (Upstream to Orchestrator)"
event_envelope_fields.note: What each emitted event SHOULD include. Payload fields beyond these are event-specific.

entries.note: The neutral token-usage record (`token_usage_fields`), with any adapter-specific counts in an opaque extras field.

log_context_fields.note: REQUIRED log context, by what the log is about. Section 18.1.1 makes structured logs carrying all three a conformance item for every implementation.

entries.required_for: logs describing a call that reached the code host
entries.note: Names the scope the call's credential came from — a repository, or the orchestrator level — never the credential or any part of its value (Sections 8.7, 15.3).

The run attempt whose failure produced this one (Sections 7.2, 8.4, 13.1). Names the origin of a retry sequence rather than the immediate predecessor, so the sequence is a group rather than a linked list. Always present: the first attempt of a run is its own origin.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 13.5 "Session Metrics and Token Accounting"
token_usage_fields.note: The neutral token-usage record each adapter normalizes its protocol's usage payloads into. Absolute cumulative totals, never deltas (Section 13.5); adapter-specific counts such as cache tokens go in an extras field rather than here.

ledger_entry_fields.note: One entry of the OPTIONAL per-execution usage ledger: a full absolute snapshot of one session's token usage at one observation. Entries are keyed by (`issue_identifier`, `session_id`); `required: true` marks a field whose absence makes the entry invalid and MUST be skipped on read.

recovery_classes.note: Every Orchestrator Runtime State field (Section 4.1.8), and any state an OPTIONAL extension introduces, MUST be assigned exactly one class, published in the Conformance Statement (Section 19).

runtime_state_fields.note: The single authoritative runtime state and the recovery class Section 4.1.8 states for each field. An implementation records its own assignment in its Conformance Statement (Section 19); this is the specification's, which is what that record is compared against.

entries.note: Becomes `Durable` when a budgeting extension enforces on it, and is then Symphony-attributed rather than account-wide.

The per-repository backoff Section 14.2 requires where an engine policy could not be used at all. Carries no park state: whether persistent failures are parked is `Implementation-defined`, so a park record is Core-introduced state governed by Section 14.3 rather than a field this enumeration shapes.

Observability in Core, where the reset consequence is that the status surface reports no rate-limit reading until the next agent update refreshes it. Becomes `Cached external signal` when the OPTIONAL provider-quota extension (Section 8.9) enforces on it, which is where its staleness bound and its `UNKNOWN` policy come from. An absent value denotes `UNKNOWN`, distinct from any reading and in particular not `0`.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 18.2 "RECOMMENDED Extensions (Not REQUIRED for Conformance)"
config_namespaces.note: Top-level configuration keys and the artifact each belongs to (Section 5). `core: true` marks a key the core schema defines; the rest are owned by the OPTIONAL extension named in `spec_ref`, and an implementation publishes the namespaces it ships in its Conformance Statement (Section 19). Not a closed set: Section 5.3 permits an extension to define additional top-level keys.

entries.note: Its `transitions` field is repository-owned and lives in `repo.policy.toml` (Section 11.6).
In-sandbox hooks in `WORKFLOW.md`, host-side hooks in `repo.policy.toml` (Section 15.4).
Owned by the OPTIONAL forge budget guard. Only the guard is optional: recording the snapshot the engine reports on every forge-touching operation is Core and requires none of this namespace's keys.
Reserved for observability settings (Section 13); the specification names the namespace, not the fields. Ledger settings are `observability.ledger.*` (Section 13.6).
Section 13.8 starts the HTTP server when a CLI `--port` argument is given or `server.port` is present in `WORKFLOW.md` front matter.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 5.5 "Workflow Validation and Error Surface"
SPEC.md Section 5.1 "WORKFLOW.md Discovery and Path Resolution"
error_classes.note: The classes the workflow loader and the prompt renderer fail with. A class names the condition, not the stage at which an implementation detects it: an unknown variable and an unknown filter are both `template_render_error` however early the template engine resolves them, and `template_parse_error` is reserved for a body that is not well-formed template syntax at all. `gating` is Section 5.5's dispatch gating behavior, which is the part a consumer acts on (Sections 6.2, 12.4): `blocks_dispatch` holds new dispatches until the file is repaired, `fails_attempt` fails only the affected run attempt. Not a closed set: Section 5.5 permits an implementation to define additional classes for conditions these five do not name, and requires it to document each one and assign it a gating behavior.

entries.condition: The workflow file cannot be read at the resolved path (Section 5.1).
The YAML front matter is not well-formed (Section 5.2).
The front matter is well-formed YAML that does not decode to a map (Section 5.2).
The prompt body is not well-formed template syntax.
The body is well formed and names something the engine cannot resolve: an unknown variable, an unknown filter, or an invalid interpolation (Section 5.4).

tracker_error_categories.note: Transport-neutral categories each tracker adapter maps its transport's failures onto. RECOMMENDED, so the names are a target vocabulary rather than a checked spelling; a generated type MUST admit an unknown token. The first three entries carry no `condition` because Section 11.4 states none. Section 17.3 requires four of them by name in `Core Conformance` checks — `tracker_unsupported_operation`, `tracker_state_unreachable`, `tracker_state_conflict`, `tracker_pagination_error` — which is a disagreement with this level recorded in `conformance/README.md` rather than resolved here.

entries.condition: Write not in the adapter capability descriptor (Section 11.7).
`set_state` target unreachable from the current state (Section 11.8).
Issue state changed underneath a `set_state` write (Section 11.8).
Transport or connection failure.
Unsuccessful response status, for example non-2xx HTTP.
Backend-reported errors in a well-formed response, for example a GraphQL `errors` array.
Unexpected or unparseable response payload.
Pagination integrity failure, for example a missing continuation cursor.

agent_error_categories.note: Normalized categories an agent adapter maps its protocol's failures onto. RECOMMENDED, so the names are a target vocabulary rather than a checked spelling; a generated type MUST admit an unknown token. Section 10.6 states no condition for any of them. `turn_failed`, `turn_cancelled` and `turn_input_required` are also `events` entries (Section 10.4): the category is named after the event that produced it, so a generator emitting one type per group has three names in two enums by design rather than by collision.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 11.6 "Workflow State Machine and Transition Triggers"
transition_triggers.note: The closed vocabulary a repository's `tracker.transitions` draws each entry's `on` value from. Three origins: agent-emitted milestone signals, orchestrator-observed run outcomes, and the OPTIONAL task-state events (`core: false`). This is Symphony's vocabulary and Symphony is its authority. `tracker.transitions` travels in `repo.policy.toml` because the repository owns the wiring, but `set_state` is a consumer-effected action over a tracker outside the VCS/forge domain, so the engine carries and validates the table without matching its `on` (`VCSX-SPEC.md` Sections 5.2, 6.7) — its own triggers are the two kinds it produces itself, a lifecycle position and a typed operation result. That is why the tokens below include conditions no engine operation reports, and why `pull_request_opened` names a pull request opened during the run by any means rather than one operation's result. REQUIRED rather than RECOMMENDED because Section 6.3 rejects an `on` outside this set — a check Symphony MUST make itself, since nothing downstream would catch a misspelled trigger: it binds no transition and fires nothing, which is indistinguishable from a trigger that simply never occurred.

entries.condition: The agent signals through the broker CLI that the work is ready for review.
The agent signals that it is blocked.
The agent signals that the work is done.
The orchestrator has claimed the issue and started its first turn (Sections 7.1, 7.3).
A pull request was opened for the issue during the run.
The run attempt finished in `Succeeded` (Section 7.2).
The run attempt finished in a failure terminal reason — `Failed`, `TimedOut` or `Stalled` (Section 7.2).
The retry path completed without re-dispatch (Sections 7.1 `Released`, 8.4).
Every implementation task for the issue is closed; the daemon's computed-completion trigger (Section 8.10).
An agent-created human-assigned task parks the run for feedback (Section 8.10). The `#` names a condition across tasks, not a proto class.

failure_classes.note: The classes a failure is classified to. Section 14.1 gives each a `name` for prose and a `token` an implementation classifies to and a Conformance Statement is keyed by; the token is REQUIRED, so two implementations reporting the same condition report the same token. `core: false` marks the two the OPTIONAL node-scheduler extension defines (Section 9.11). Not a closed set: Section 14.1 permits an OPTIONAL extension to define additional categories and requires it to document each one and its recovery disposition — the specification's own example is the budget extension's `token_budget_exceeded` (Section 8.8), which names a condition rather than a class of them and so is not spelled like these nine. Openness is a property of the set, not of the names: an implementation shipping no such extension classifies to exactly these nine and MAY close its own enum there. The Section 14.2 recovery disposition is deliberately not carried here — it is the prose of a rule rather than a property Section 14.1 fixes about a token, and the mapping is not one-to-one (`workspace_failures` and `agent_session_failures` share one disposition, `tracker_failures` takes two). Section 14.2 names the classes each of its bullets disposes of.

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 3.4 "Layers, the VCS Engine, and Deployment Topologies"
layer_profiles.note: The two profiles `Core Conformance` comprises, one per layer that has one. A deployment claims the ones its topology composes (`deployment_topologies`), and Section 19 makes the claim a field of its Conformance Statement — which is the reader this group serves: the spelling is what a consumer reads to learn what an implementation asserts about itself, so it is published rather than transcribed. Closed: Section 17 states that `Core Conformance` "comprises two layer profiles". The VCS engine layer has no profile here, its obligations being the engine contract's (Sections 3.4, 17), so the set has two members and not three. Written in the specification's capitalization, which is what a Statement reproduces.

entries.condition: The secret-isolation invariant and the per-run execution boundary: the per-run broker socket and scope guard, the sandbox, the secret split, the executor, the workspace manager, the agent runner and its adapters, and the broker-mediated tracker writes. Independently conformant — satisfiable for a single agent session in a workspace that already exists.
The autonomous layer: polling, candidate selection and enumeration, concurrency, retry, reconciliation, multi-repository routing, the tracker read surface, and the workflow file and prompt template.

validation_profiles.note: The profiles a check belongs to. Section 18 uses the same four for the checklist, so the names span the test matrix and the definition of done. `Core Conformance` is the one that decomposes: it comprises the two `layer_profiles`, and a claim names those rather than this. Requirement level varies by member and is carried per entry rather than for the group, which is why the group states none: `Core Conformance` is REQUIRED of every implementation, `Extension Conformance` is REQUIRED only for an OPTIONAL feature an implementation ships, and the last two are RECOMMENDED — both being environment-dependent in a way the deterministic corpus is not.

entries.condition: Deterministic tests REQUIRED for all conforming implementations. Comprises the two `layer_profiles`; an implementation claims the ones its topology composes.
REQUIRED only for OPTIONAL features an implementation chooses to ship. Each OPTIONAL feature declares the layer profile it extends.
Environment-dependent smoke and integration checks, RECOMMENDED before production use (Section 17.8).

Several sessions run concurrently against one repository and one pull request, asserting that every mutating forge write either applies to the pull-request identity its session established or is refused (Sections 9.10, 17.9).

spec_refs: SPEC.md Section 3.4 "Layers, the VCS Engine, and Deployment Topologies"
deployment_topologies.note: The three ways the layers compose into a deployment. Section 19 makes the topology a field of the Conformance Statement, which is this group's reader. Closed: Section 3.4 states "Three deployment topologies compose the layers". `claims` carries the layer profiles each topology asserts — `engine-direct` claims none defined by `SPEC.md`, having no Broker Core and no daemon, which is a value a generated type has to admit rather than an omission. Conformance follows the layers rather than the topologies (Section 3.4), so a topology is what an implementation reports and a profile is what it is held to.

entries.condition: The autonomous daemon over the Broker Core, driving the VCS Engine. The full service this specification describes.
The Broker Core plus the VCS Engine's `ship`/`land`, driving one interactive agent session with no polling daemon.

The VCS Engine alone, run directly by an operator who holds the credentials, with no Broker Core sandbox. Outside the agent-secret-isolation model, and therefore claiming no profile defined in `SPEC.md`.
